paragraphes: Your school cafeteria does not make everything itself. The bread comes from a bakery, the meat from a farmer, the yogurts from a factory.
One day, a single batch of yogurts is spoiled at the supplier. Nobody in the cafeteria did anything wrong. Still, half the school gets sick.
Companies live the same thing with their equipment, their programs and their services. We call it supply chain risk.

decouverte.comme: A bike chain holds as long as every link holds. One rusty link, and it breaks.
decouverte.enVrai: The supply chain is made of all the suppliers a company depends on. They deliver hardware (the machines you can touch), software (programs) or services. Each supplier (also called a vendor) is a link. The image stops here: you can see a rusty link, but a risk at a supplier often stays invisible.

decouverte.question: Your school picks a new yogurt supplier. What does it do before signing?
options: It checks how the supplier works
It picks the cheapest one
It trusts a well-known name
decouverte.answer: It checks how the supplier works
decouverte.explanation: The school trusts someone else with part of its students' health. So it must check. Price and reputation are tempting, but they prove nothing about quality.

decouverte.texte: A company wants to store its data with a cloud provider (CSP, cloud service provider). This is a company that rents out its servers over the internet. The provider keeps the data in another country. The law of your country may forbid that. There is no hacker here: the risk comes from a compliance rule (a rule of law or contract) that is not followed.

cards.question: Official definition: “supply chain”
cards.answer: Securing your organization's assets requires that you evaluate the security risk of your entire supply chain and that you apply appropriate controls to manage that risk.
cards.explanation: Two moves: measure the risk at all suppliers, then take action.
cards.explanation_more: Sentence from the official manual (ISC)2, Domain 1, section “Apply Supply Chain Risk Management Concepts”. An asset is anything of value to the company: data, machines, software.

cards.question: Securing your organization's assets requires that you [[evaluate the security risk]] of your [[entire supply chain]] and that you [[apply appropriate controls]] to manage that risk.
cards.answer: Securing your organization's assets requires that you evaluate the security risk of your entire supply chain and that you apply appropriate controls to manage that risk.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: evaluate the risk, look at the whole chain, apply the right controls.

cards.question: What is the supply chain in cybersecurity?
cards.answer: All the suppliers a company depends on: hardware, software and services. If one link is weak, everything after it is exposed.
cards.explanation: Think of the cafeteria: one spoiled batch makes everyone sick.

cards.question: A cloud provider keeps your data in a country where the law forbids it. What kind of risk is this?
options: A compliance risk
A hardware failure risk
cards.answer: A compliance risk
cards.explanation: No machine breaks down: a rule of law is not being followed.
cards.explanation_more: The manual gives this case: data stored outside the country. Source: Domain 1, section “Risks Associated with Hardware, Software, and Services”.

cards.question: Your company wants to add a program bought from a software vendor. What should it look at first?
options: Its effect on overall security
First, the number of computers to equip
The promises the vendor advertises
Its release date on the market
options_why: The number of computers matters less than the impact on security.
A promise is not proof: you have to check.
A recent product can hide risks too.
cards.answer: Its effect on overall security
cards.explanation: Before adding something that comes from a third party, you look at how it fits in. You also look at what it changes for security.
cards.explanation_more: Source: official manual (ISC)2, Domain 1, section “Risks Associated with Hardware, Software, and Services”.

cards.question: A company must evaluate the risk of its whole [[supply chain]], not only of its own machines.
cards.answer: A company must evaluate the risk of its whole supply chain, not only of its own machines.
cards.explanation: A risk can reach you through any supplier.

cards.question: Why can a company not protect only its own computers?
cards.answer: Because it depends on its suppliers. If one of them is hacked or careless, the problem reaches the company. It comes through the hardware, the software or the service delivered.
cards.explanation: A weak link elsewhere becomes a weak link at your place.

cards.question: Which family does each supplier example belong to?
cards.answer: Hardware: laptops and hard drives. Software: the word processor and the email program. Service: hosting with a cloud provider and the payroll company.
cards.explanation: You can touch hardware, you install software, and a service is provided by an outside company.

items.text: Laptops bought in bulk
Hard drives for the servers
A word processor bought with its license
An email program installed on every computer
Hosting a website with a cloud provider
A company that calculates the pay

cards.question: What does CSP stand for?
cards.answer: Cloud service provider: a company that rents out its servers over the internet.
cards.explanation: It is one more supplier in your supply chain.

cards.question: What if your cloud provider does not meet the security requirements that the law or your contract gives you?
cards.answer: Your company runs a security risk, because it no longer meets its own obligations. So you must check before signing.
cards.explanation: The legal and contract duties stay yours, even if the provider takes care of the servers.
cards.explanation_more: The manual gives this case: a cloud provider that does not meet legal or contract requirements.

cards.question: Name two possible risks when you use a cloud provider.
cards.answer: A compliance risk if the data is stored outside the country. A security risk if the provider does not meet legal or contract requirements.
cards.explanation: Both come from the fact that you trust data to a third party.

cards.question: Your company wants to rent a cloud service. Write two questions to ask the provider before signing.
cards.answer: Where will my data be stored, in which country? Do you meet the security requirements that the law or my contract gives me?
cards.explanation: These two questions cover the risks named in the manual.

concepts.name: Malicious code in the supply chain

paragraphes: Your phone offers you an update. You tap Install without thinking, because it comes from the maker of the app.
Imagine a hacker slipped a trap into that update before it was sent. The trap could be a Trojan, a hidden program inside normal software. Everyone would install it.
The victim is no longer attacked directly, but their supplier is. This is a supply chain attack.

decouverte.comme: A letter carries the post office stamp. If someone slips a trap into the envelope before the stamp, everyone will think the letter is official.
decouverte.enVrai: A software vendor signs its updates (code signing): it is a digital stamp that proves they come from the vendor. If the trap is added before the signature, the stamp stays valid. The image stops here: the stamp proves where the update comes from, not that it is free of traps.

decouverte.question: In 2017, an official update of a well-known program contained a Trojan. Why did so many people install it?
options: It came from the vendor itself
It promised money
It arrived in an email from a stranger
decouverte.answer: It came from the vendor itself
decouverte.explanation: Users trusted the vendor. Here, trust was the weak spot. Promises of money and emails from strangers trap people too, but not in this case.

decouverte.texte: The maker of the CCleaner program sends its users a routine update. It contains a remote-access Trojan. This gives the attacker control of the computer from far away. The trapped code was added before the signature. The manual mentions more than 2 billion downloads.

In 2020, the company FireEye reveals a giant attack, called SUNBURST. It goes through Orion, a SolarWinds product used to watch and manage computer systems. The tool meant to protect became the weapon. Victims include Microsoft, Intel, U.S. government agencies and FireEye itself. SolarWinds estimates about 18,000 companies were affected.

cards.question: Official definition: “COTS” software
cards.answer: The widespread use of proprietary commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) software requires customers to trust the security practices of the vendors.
cards.explanation: COTS software is bought ready-made: you cannot see how it is built, so you trust.
cards.explanation_more: Definition from the official manual (ISC)2, Domain 1, section “Malicious Code in the Supply Chain”. “Off-the-shelf” means taken straight from the store shelf, like a boxed game.

cards.question: The widespread use of [[proprietary commercial off-the-shelf]] (COTS) software requires [[customers to trust]] the [[security practices]] of the vendors.
cards.answer: The widespread use of proprietary commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) software requires customers to trust the security practices of the vendors.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: store-bought software, the customer's trust, the vendor's practices.

cards.question: Official definition: “SUNBURST”
cards.answer: SUNBURST is a vulnerability within the SolarWinds Orion Platform, which, if present and activated, allows an attacker to compromise the server on which the Orion product is running.
cards.explanation: A hidden weakness in a trusted tool, which opens the door to attackers.
cards.explanation_more: Definition from the official manual (ISC)2, Domain 1. The attack was revealed in 2020 by the company FireEye.

cards.question: SUNBURST is a [[vulnerability within]] the SolarWinds Orion Platform, which, [[if present and activated]], allows an attacker to [[compromise the server]] on which the Orion product is running.
cards.answer: SUNBURST is a vulnerability within the SolarWinds Orion Platform, which, if present and activated, allows an attacker to compromise the server on which the Orion product is running.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: the weakness, the condition (present and activated), the result (the server is compromised).

cards.question: What makes an attack through a software vendor so effective?
cards.answer: The updates come from a trusted source. Users install them without suspicion, so the trap spreads everywhere.
cards.explanation: Trust in the vendor becomes the way in.
cards.explanation_more: The manual says this method is popular with malware authors. The updates come from a trusted source.

cards.question: A company installs the official update of its accounting software. It contained trapped code. What was mainly used against the company?
options: Trust in the software vendor
A password that was too weak
A misleading email sent to an employee
A weakness in the company's firewall
options_why: No password is involved: the trap came through the update.
No employee was fooled by an email: the update looked official.
The trap came in through the trusted software, not by breaking through the firewall.
cards.answer: Trust in the software vendor
cards.explanation: The company installed the update because it trusted its supplier.

cards.question: Which situation is a supply chain attack?
options: A trap hidden in an official update
A misleading email sent to an employee
cards.answer: A trap hidden in an official update
cards.explanation: In the first case, the attacker goes through the supplier. In the second, they aim directly at the person.

cards.question: Why did the trapped code in CCleaner pass as a real update?
cards.answer: The malicious code was inserted before the signature. So the whole update package looked official to users.
cards.explanation: The signature proves where the package comes from, not that its content is safe.
cards.explanation_more: Source: official manual (ISC)2, Domain 1, section “Malicious Code in the Supply Chain”.

cards.question: In [[2017]], the CCleaner update contained a remote-access Trojan.
cards.answer: In 2017, the CCleaner update contained a remote-access Trojan.
cards.explanation: A routine update, yet it was trapped.
cards.explanation_more: Source: official manual (ISC)2, Domain 1. The manual mentions more than 2 billion downloads. This is the figure given by the book.

cards.question: Which product was trapped in the SUNBURST attack?
cards.answer: Orion, a SolarWinds product used to watch and manage computer systems.
cards.explanation: Irony: the tool meant to watch the systems became the attacker's tool.

cards.question: In which attack does each detail belong?
cards.answer: CCleaner: Trojan delivered, code added before the signature, more than 2 billion downloads. SolarWinds: trapped monitoring tool, announced by FireEye, about 18,000 companies affected.
cards.explanation: CCleaner dates from 2017 and involves a signed update. SolarWinds dates from 2020 and involves a monitoring tool.

items.text: A remote-access Trojan is delivered in the update
The trapped code was added before the signature
More than 2 billion downloads (figure from the manual)
The trapped tool is used to watch computer systems
FireEye revealed the attack, then found it was a victim too
About 18,000 companies affected

cards.question: Which company revealed the SUNBURST attack, in 2020?
cards.answer: FireEye, which was also a victim of it.
cards.explanation: Even a top cybersecurity company can be hit.
cards.explanation_more: Source: official manual (ISC)2, Domain 1, section “SolarWinds and the SUNBURST Attack”.

cards.question: SolarWinds estimates that about [[18,000|18000|eighteen thousand]] companies were affected worldwide.
cards.answer: SolarWinds estimates that about 18,000 companies were affected worldwide.
cards.explanation: One single trapped product hit thousands of companies.
cards.explanation_more: Source: official manual (ISC)2, Domain 1, section “SolarWinds and the SUNBURST Attack”.

cards.question: What if you learn that the tool that watches your computer systems is itself trapped?
cards.answer: Then the trap has very wide access to your systems. That tool is everywhere and has your trust. This is what made SUNBURST so serious.
cards.explanation: A monitoring tool sees everything: if it is trapped, the attacker sees everything too.

cards.question: You are in charge of security at a company. Write one thing to do to lower the risk of a trapped software vendor.
cards.answer: Evaluate the vendor's security practices before buying, then re-evaluate and monitor the vendor regularly.
cards.explanation: You cannot check everything, but you can choose your suppliers and follow them.

paragraphes: The school changes caterer for the end-of-year party. The caterer promises perfect meals. The principal believes the promise.
On the big day, everyone finds out the kitchen is not clean. If someone had visited it before, they would have seen it.
When a company gives work to a third party (an outside company), it must check first, then keep watching. This is third-party assessment and monitoring.

decouverte.comme: Before hiring the caterer, the principal visits the kitchen and reads its hygiene reports. Later, the principal comes back from time to time.
decouverte.enVrai: The company does the same with its suppliers. It checks their security before signing. Then it re-evaluates them regularly and monitors them all the time. The image stops here: you cannot always visit a supplier on the other side of the world. That is why the manual says “where feasible”, which means when it is possible.

decouverte.question: The caterer passed the inspection in January. Should you still keep watching in June?
options: Yes, you check again regularly
No, one inspection is enough
Only after an accident
decouverte.explanation: A supplier changes: new employees, new methods. The manual asks you to re-evaluate regularly and to monitor continuously. Waiting for an accident is tempting, but then it is too late.

decouverte.texte: To check a supplier, the manual names three activities. The onsite security survey: a visit to look at its security on the spot. The formal security audit: a step-by-step review of its systems. Penetration testing: experts, with permission, try to break into its systems to find weak spots.

A company wants to hire a payroll provider. It compares the provider's practices with its own security requirements. An access control is missing? The company writes down this gap and follows it closely.

cards.question: Official definition: “third-party risk management policy”
cards.answer: Any organization that does business with contractors, vendors, or any other third parties should have a third-party risk management policy that establishes a third-party risk management program responsible for assessing, monitoring, and controlling risks associated with outsourcing to third parties.
cards.explanation: Three verbs to remember: assess, monitor, control.
cards.explanation_more: Sentence from the official manual (ISC)2, Domain 1, section “Third-Party Assessment and Monitoring”. Outsourcing means giving a task to an outside company.

cards.question: Any organization that does business with contractors, vendors, or any other third parties should have a third-party risk management [[policy]] that establishes a third-party risk management [[program]] responsible for assessing, monitoring, and controlling risks associated with outsourcing to third parties.
cards.answer: Any organization that does business with contractors, vendors, or any other third parties should have a third-party risk management policy that establishes a third-party risk management program responsible for assessing, monitoring, and controlling risks associated with outsourcing to third parties.
cards.explanation: The policy decides, the program acts.

cards.question: Any organization that does business with [[contractors, vendors]], or any other third parties should have a [[third-party risk management policy]] that establishes a third-party risk management program responsible for [[assessing, monitoring, and controlling]] risks associated with outsourcing to third parties.
cards.answer: Any organization that does business with contractors, vendors, or any other third parties should have a third-party risk management policy that establishes a third-party risk management program responsible for assessing, monitoring, and controlling risks associated with outsourcing to third parties.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: who you work with, the policy, and the three verbs of the program.

cards.question: Write the official definition of “third-party risk management policy” from memory.
cards.answer: Any organization that does business with contractors, vendors, or any other third parties should have a third-party risk management policy that establishes a third-party risk management program responsible for assessing, monitoring, and controlling risks associated with outsourcing to third parties.
cards.explanation: Start with “Any organization...”, then look for policy, program, and the three verbs.

cards.question: Official definition: the activities for overseeing third parties
cards.answer: Governance and oversight activities should include onsite security surveys, formal security audits of third-party systems, and penetration testing, where feasible.
cards.explanation: Three checks: visit, audit, test. And always “where feasible”: when it is possible.
cards.explanation_more: Sentence from the official manual (ISC)2, Domain 1. The manual points to chapter 6 for audits.

cards.question: Governance and oversight activities should include [[onsite security surveys]], [[formal security audits]] of third-party systems, and [[penetration testing]], where feasible.
cards.answer: Governance and oversight activities should include onsite security surveys, formal security audits of third-party systems, and penetration testing, where feasible.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: the visit, the audit, the penetration test.

cards.question: Official definition: assessing a new third party
cards.answer: Any new third party should be assessed against your organization's security requirements, and gaps should be documented and closely monitored.
cards.explanation: Assess, write down the gaps, follow them closely.
cards.explanation_more: Sentence from the official manual (ISC)2, Domain 1, section “Third-Party Assessment and Monitoring”.

cards.question: Any new third party should be [[assessed against]] your organization's [[security requirements]], and gaps should be [[documented and closely monitored]].
cards.answer: Any new third party should be assessed against your organization's security requirements, and gaps should be documented and closely monitored.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: the assessment, the reference (your requirements), what happens to the gaps.

cards.question: According to the manual, what is the biggest challenge with suppliers?
cards.answer: Making sure that third parties really do what they must do to protect the company's information.
cards.explanation: The good controls already exist. The hard part is getting the third party to apply them.
cards.explanation_more: Source: official manual (ISC)2, Domain 1, section “Third-Party Assessment and Monitoring”.

cards.question: Which of these two actions is a penetration test?
options: Experts try to break into the systems
You read the supplier's report
cards.answer: Experts try to break into the systems
cards.explanation: A penetration test is done for real, with permission. Reading a report only means believing what it says.

cards.question: A new supplier lacks two controls that your company requires. What do you do?
options: I write down these gaps and follow them
I ignore these gaps: the supplier is new
I refuse all suppliers
I wait for the first incident
options_why: A new supplier must be assessed like all the others.
Refusing everyone is not the solution: you document and you monitor.
Waiting for the incident means acting too late.
cards.answer: I write down these gaps and follow them
cards.explanation: The manual asks you to document the gaps and to monitor them closely.

cards.question: Which checking activity matches each description?
cards.answer: Onsite visit: looking at its buildings and servers. Formal audit: a step-by-step review with a report. Penetration test: playing the attacker with permission.
cards.explanation: Visit = you look on the spot. Audit = you review against criteria. Penetration test = you try to get in.

items.text: An expert goes to the supplier and observes its security on the spot
You look on the spot at how its buildings and servers are protected
A formal, step-by-step review of the third party's systems
A check against precise criteria, with an official report
Experts try to break into the systems to find weak spots
You play the role of an attacker, with the supplier's permission

cards.question: Suppliers must be [[re-evaluated]] regularly and [[monitored]] continuously.
cards.answer: Suppliers must be re-evaluated regularly and monitored continuously.
cards.explanation: One single check at the start is not enough.

cards.question: Why re-evaluate a supplier that was already checked?
cards.answer: Because a supplier changes: its teams, its tools and its practices change. Only regular follow-up and continuous monitoring show whether it still protects your information well.
cards.explanation: A good check in January guarantees nothing for June.

cards.question: What does the manual say about the gaps found at a new third party?
cards.answer: They must be documented, which means written down, and closely monitored.
cards.explanation: A known gap that is followed is less dangerous than a forgotten gap.

cards.question: Put in order the steps to take with a new supplier.
cards.answer:
1. Assess the third party against the security requirements
2. Document the gaps found
3. Monitor these gaps closely
4. Re-evaluate the third party regularly
5. Monitor it continuously
cards.explanation: First you assess, you write down, then you follow. The follow-up never stops.

items: Assess the third party against the security requirements

cards.question: What if your company cannot visit a supplier located in another country?
cards.answer: The manual asks for these checks “where feasible”, which means when it is possible. You then choose the checks that are still possible.
cards.explanation: The words “when it is possible” admit that not every check can always be done.

cards.question: Your company will give its payroll to a provider. Write three actions to limit the risk.
cards.answer: Assess the provider before signing, document and follow the gaps, then re-evaluate and monitor the provider regularly.
cards.explanation: Assess, follow the gaps, re-evaluate: the full cycle of third-party follow-up.

paragraphes: The school chooses its meal suppliers. Still, it sets a starting rule: every supplier keeps meat cold and cleans its kitchens.
A supplier can do better. If it does less, it is not accepted.
For a company, this starting rule is called a minimum security requirement (MSR).

decouverte.comme: In the high jump, the bar is set at a minimum height. You can jump higher, but you cannot go under it.
decouverte.enVrai: An MSR is that bar. It sets the lowest level of security the company accepts from a supplier. The supplier can do better, never less. The image stops here: the bar does not say how high to aim, only the floor to respect.

decouverte.question: A law sets a security rule. Your company wants an MSR weaker than this law. Is that allowed?
options: No: an MSR cannot be below the law
Yes: the company makes its own rules
Yes, if the supplier is small
decouverte.answer: No: an MSR cannot be below the law
decouverte.explanation: The manual says never to go below an outside requirement, such as a law, a contract or a regulation. Being the boss at home is tempting, but the law comes first.

decouverte.texte: A clinic must follow a law that protects health data. It writes its MSRs for its suppliers. It cannot set requirements weaker than the law. It must also check, with an audit, that each supplier follows them.

cards.question: Official definition: “minimum security requirements (MSRs)”
cards.answer: Similar to baselines and standards (discussed earlier in this chapter), your organization should establish minimum security requirements (MSRs) that define the least acceptable security standards that vendors and other parties in your supply chain must satisfy.
cards.explanation: Key words: “least acceptable”, the lowest level you accept.
cards.explanation_more: Sentence from the official manual (ISC)2, Domain 1, section “Minimum Security Requirements”. Baselines and standards are the security rules a company sets for its own systems.

cards.question: Similar to baselines and standards (discussed earlier in this chapter), your organization should establish [[minimum]] security requirements (MSRs) that define the [[least]] acceptable security standards that vendors and other parties in your supply chain must satisfy.
cards.answer: Similar to baselines and standards (discussed earlier in this chapter), your organization should establish minimum security requirements (MSRs) that define the least acceptable security standards that vendors and other parties in your supply chain must satisfy.
cards.explanation: Two words for the floor: “minimum” and “least acceptable”.

cards.question: Similar to baselines and standards (discussed earlier in this chapter), your organization should [[establish minimum security requirements]] (MSRs) that define the [[least acceptable security standards]] that [[vendors and other parties]] in your supply chain must satisfy.
cards.answer: Similar to baselines and standards (discussed earlier in this chapter), your organization should establish minimum security requirements (MSRs) that define the least acceptable security standards that vendors and other parties in your supply chain must satisfy.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: set the MSRs, the lowest level accepted, who they apply to.

cards.question: Write the official definition of “minimum security requirements (MSRs)” from memory.
cards.answer: Similar to baselines and standards (discussed earlier in this chapter), your organization should establish minimum security requirements (MSRs) that define the least acceptable security standards that vendors and other parties in your supply chain must satisfy.
cards.explanation: Follow the order: set the MSRs, define the floor, say who must meet it.

cards.question: Official definition: what an MSR describes
cards.answer: Of course, you should strive to ensure that your third parties have the strongest possible security postures, but MSRs, as the name suggests, describe the lowest level of security that your organization is willing to accept from a third party.
cards.explanation: You aim for the strongest, but the MSR only says the lowest level you accept.
cards.explanation_more: Sentence from the official manual (ISC)2, Domain 1. A security posture is the overall state of security, like the fitness of an athlete.

cards.question: Of course, you should strive to ensure that your third parties have the [[strongest possible]] security postures, but MSRs, as the name suggests, describe the [[lowest level of security]] that your organization is [[willing to accept]] from a third party.
cards.answer: Of course, you should strive to ensure that your third parties have the strongest possible security postures, but MSRs, as the name suggests, describe the lowest level of security that your organization is willing to accept from a third party.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: you aim for the strongest, the MSR is the lowest, which the organization accepts.

cards.question: What does the abbreviation MSR stand for?
cards.answer: Minimum security requirements: the lowest security requirements a supplier must meet.
cards.explanation: Think of the high jump bar: a floor level.

cards.question: An MSR describes the level of security that the company...
options: Accepts at the very least from a third party
Hopes for at best from a third party
cards.answer: Accepts at the very least from a third party
cards.explanation: An MSR is a floor, not an ideal goal.

cards.question: A law requires a supplier to encrypt data. Your company writes its MSR. What is the right idea?
options: Require encryption, at least as the law does
Say nothing about encryption, because it is expensive
Ask for less than the law, to stay flexible
Let each supplier decide alone
options_why: Silence leaves the supplier free not to encrypt: the law would not be followed.
An MSR must not be below an outside requirement, such as the law.
Without a shared rule, there is no floor anymore.
cards.answer: Require encryption, at least as the law does
cards.explanation: An MSR takes into account legal, contract and regulatory requirements. It never goes below them.
cards.explanation_more: Source: official manual (ISC)2, Domain 1, section “Minimum Security Requirements”.

cards.question: An MSR describes the [[lowest]] level of security that the company accepts from a third party.
cards.answer: An MSR describes the lowest level of security that the company accepts from a third party.
cards.explanation: The floor, not the ceiling.

cards.question: Why must an MSR take laws and contracts into account?
cards.answer: Because the company must follow these outside requirements. An MSR weaker than the law would put the company in breach, even if the supplier follows its own rules.
cards.explanation: The law comes before internal rules.
cards.explanation_more: The manual says: do not set an MSR below an outside compliance requirement.

cards.question: Your MSR says: “encrypt data and keep logs”. Which suppliers are accepted?
cards.answer: Accepted: the one that encrypts and keeps logs, the one that does this and adds a double check. Refused: the one that keeps logs without encrypting, the one that encrypts without logs.
cards.explanation: You must reach the floor. Doing more is allowed, doing less is not.

items.text: Encrypts data and keeps logs
Encrypts data, keeps logs and adds a double check
Keeps logs but does not encrypt data
Encrypts data but keeps no logs

cards.question: What must the company do after setting and sharing its MSRs?
cards.answer: Be ready to audit and assess how well third parties meet these MSRs.
cards.explanation: A rule without checks does not protect.
cards.explanation_more: Source: official manual (ISC)2, Domain 1, section “Minimum Security Requirements”.

cards.question: What if a supplier is much better than the MSR?
cards.answer: No problem: the MSR is the lowest level accepted. The manual even advises aiming for the strongest security postures possible.
cards.explanation: The floor does not stop anyone from going higher.

cards.question: Write an example of an MSR for a computer supplier of your school.
cards.answer: For example: “All student data must be encrypted.” An MSR sets a threshold that every supplier must meet.
cards.explanation: A good MSR is precise and can be checked by an audit.

paragraphes: Your school signs a contract with the cafeteria. It says: meals are served before half past noon, every day.
A month later, meals arrive at two o'clock. The school shows the contract and demands a remedy.
In computing, this kind of contract is called a service-level agreement (SLA).

decouverte.comme: A pizza driver promises: “in 30 minutes, or it's free”. If the pizza is late, you have rights.
decouverte.enVrai: An SLA works the same way. The supplier promises a minimum level of performance, written in a contract. If it does not keep the promise, the customer has rights. The image stops here: an SLA is a signed, precise contract, not just a spoken promise.

decouverte.question: Your cloud provider is down for a long time. Your SLA promises a system that works almost all the time. What can it give you?
options: Compensation, or leaving without a penalty
Nothing: a breakdown is normal
An apology, that's all
decouverte.answer: Compensation, or leaving without a penalty
decouverte.explanation: The SLA is a contract: the supplier must keep its promise. If not, the customer can get money or end the service without a penalty.

decouverte.texte: A company rents servers from a cloud provider. The SLA promises a level of system availability (uptime: the time when the service works). If there is a long outage, the company can receive financial compensation. It can also stop the service without a penalty.

cards.question: Official definition: “service-level agreement (SLA)”
cards.answer: A service-level agreement (SLA) is a contractual agreement between a service provider and its customers that establishes the minimum performance standards that the provider is obligated to meet.
cards.explanation: Key words: contractual, minimum, obligated. It is the supplier's written promise.
cards.explanation_more: Definition from the official manual (ISC)2, Domain 1, section “Service-Level Requirements”.

cards.question: A service-level agreement (SLA) is a [[contractual]] agreement between a service provider and its customers that establishes the minimum performance standards that the provider is [[obligated]] to meet.
cards.answer: A service-level agreement (SLA) is a contractual agreement between a service provider and its customers that establishes the minimum performance standards that the provider is obligated to meet.
cards.explanation: A contract, and a duty: the supplier has no choice.

cards.question: A service-level agreement (SLA) is a [[contractual agreement]] between a [[service provider]] and its customers that establishes the [[minimum performance standards]] that the provider is obligated to meet.
cards.answer: A service-level agreement (SLA) is a contractual agreement between a service provider and its customers that establishes the minimum performance standards that the provider is obligated to meet.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: the contract, the two parties, the minimum performance.

cards.question: Write the official definition of “service-level agreement (SLA)” from memory.
cards.answer: A service-level agreement (SLA) is a contractual agreement between a service provider and its customers that establishes the minimum performance standards that the provider is obligated to meet.
cards.explanation: Remember the order: contract, provider and customers, minimum performance, duty.

cards.question: Official definition: what SLAs are for with third parties
cards.answer: When dealing with vendors and other third parties, SLAs serve as documented and agreed-upon performance requirements that a customer can use to hold the third party accountable.
cards.explanation: The SLA is the written proof that lets you ask for answers.
cards.explanation_more: Sentence from the official manual (ISC)2, Domain 1, section “Service-Level Requirements”.

cards.question: When dealing with vendors and other third parties, SLAs serve as [[documented and agreed-upon]] [[performance requirements]] that a customer can use to [[hold the third party accountable]].
cards.answer: When dealing with vendors and other third parties, SLAs serve as documented and agreed-upon performance requirements that a customer can use to hold the third party accountable.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: written and agreed, the performance, holding the third party responsible.

cards.question: What does SLA stand for?
cards.answer: Service-level agreement: a contract that sets the minimum performance of the supplier.
cards.explanation: It is the supplier's written promise to its customer.

cards.question: The supplier promises by contract to guarantee a level of performance. Which document is it?
options: An SLA
An MSR
cards.answer: An SLA
cards.explanation: The SLA is the supplier's promise about performance. The MSR is the security threshold set by the customer.

cards.question: Your company's website, hosted by a cloud provider, is down for several days. What do you check first?
options: The SLA signed with the provider
The password policy
The provider's yearly report
The employees' internal rules
options_why: This policy controls access to accounts, not the provider's outages.
A report describes the past and does not commit the provider to anything toward you.
These rules are about your employees, not your supplier.
cards.answer: The SLA signed with the provider
cards.explanation: The SLA says what availability the provider must deliver and what you can demand in case of an outage.

cards.question: An SLA is a [[contractual]] agreement between a service provider and its [[customers]].
cards.answer: An SLA is a contractual agreement between a service provider and its customers.
cards.explanation: A contract, not just a promise.

cards.question: Why is it in a customer's interest to have an SLA with its supplier?
cards.answer: Because the SLA sets the minimum performance in writing. If the supplier does not meet it, the customer can hold it responsible: compensation or the end of the contract.
cards.explanation: Without a written document, you cannot prove what was promised.

cards.question: SLA or MSR? Sort each sentence.
cards.answer: SLA: the supplier commits to uptime, compensation after a long outage, the signed contract. MSR: the lowest security level accepted, the bar set by the customer, the check planned by the company.
cards.explanation: The SLA comes from the supplier and is about performance. The MSR comes from the customer and is about security.

items.text: The supplier commits to a minimum uptime
Compensation is planned for a long outage
A signed contract between the supplier and its customers
The lowest level of security the company accepts
A bar that the customer sets for its suppliers
The company must be ready to check whether suppliers meet it

cards.question: What can a company get if the supplier's service is down for a long time?
cards.answer: Financial compensation, or the right to end the service without a penalty, depending on what the SLA says.
cards.explanation: This is the advantage of a written promise.
cards.explanation_more: Source: official manual (ISC)2, Domain 1, section “Service-Level Requirements”. The manual speaks of a sustained outage.

cards.question: What if you have no SLA with your cloud provider?
cards.answer: You have no document to demand a level of performance. You cannot hold the provider responsible for an outage, and you depend on its goodwill.
cards.explanation: Without a written promise, everything rests on trust.

cards.question: You choose a cloud provider. Write a performance promise that you would want to see in the SLA.
cards.answer: For example: a minimum level of system availability (uptime), with compensation after a long outage.
cards.explanation: A good promise is precise and can be measured.

concepts.name: NIST IR 7622: ten practices for the supply chain

decouverte.titre: The guide of ten good habits
paragraphes: After several stomach bug outbreaks in cafeterias, an agency publishes ten good habits to follow.
A big high school cafeteria and a small club snack bar do not apply them the same way. Each one adapts to its role.
For the supply chain of computer systems, there is a list of the same kind: NIST IR 7622. NIST is an agency of the U.S. government that publishes security guides.

decouverte.comme: Sleeping enough, moving, washing your hands: ten simple habits protect your health. An athlete and a high school student do not adapt them the same way.
decouverte.enVrai: NIST IR 7622 is a guide of ten practices to lower supply chain risk. The text says that actions change with each person's role, like the level and type of control. The image stops here: these are precise security practices, not general advice.

decouverte.question: In a chain, you are a small supplier and your neighbor is a very big manufacturer. Are your controls the same?
options: No: they depend on each one's role
Yes: everyone applies the same ones
Only the big manufacturer applies any
decouverte.answer: No: they depend on each one's role
decouverte.explanation: The manual says the actions, the level and the type of control change with the role. Everyone takes part, but not in the same way.

decouverte.texte: First practice: “Uniquely identify supply chain elements, processes, and actors”. In other words: keep a precise list of who and what makes up the chain. Last practice: “Manage disposal and final disposition activities throughout the system or element lifecycle”. In other words: even the end of life of a piece of equipment is part of security.

The U.S. government also has CNSS Directive 505 (CNSS stands for Committee on National Security Systems). It sets security requirements for national security systems. There is also initiative CNCI number 11. It gives agencies tools to manage their cyber supply chain, with an approach based on risk.

cards.question: Official definition: “NIST IR 7622”
cards.answer: The U.S. government began directly addressing cyber supply chain risk as a separate issue with the publication of NIST IR 7622, "Notional Supply Chain Risk Management Practices for Federal Information Systems."
cards.explanation: NIST IR 7622: the first U.S. text to deal with this risk separately.
cards.explanation_more: Sentence from the official manual (ISC)2, Domain 1, section “NIST IR 7622”.

cards.question: The U.S. government began [[directly addressing]] cyber supply chain risk as a [[separate issue]] with the publication of [[NIST IR 7622]], "Notional Supply Chain Risk Management Practices for Federal Information Systems."
cards.answer: The U.S. government began directly addressing cyber supply chain risk as a separate issue with the publication of NIST IR 7622, "Notional Supply Chain Risk Management Practices for Federal Information Systems."
cards.explanation: Three blocks: deal with it directly, as a separate issue, through NIST IR 7622.

cards.question: Which NIST text was the starting point for dealing with cyber supply chain risk separately?
cards.answer: NIST IR 7622, “Notional Supply Chain Risk Management Practices for Federal Information Systems”.
cards.explanation: IR stands for “interagency report”, a report from NIST.
cards.explanation_more: Source: official manual (ISC)2, Domain 1, section “NIST IR 7622”. The meaning of IR is outside the manual.

cards.question: How many practices does NIST IR 7622 identify?
options_why: Twelve is the number of principles of the British NCSC, a different source.
There are more: ten in all.
There are fewer: ten in all.
cards.explanation: Ten practices to consider when facing supply chain risk.
cards.explanation_more: Source: official manual (ISC)2, Domain 1, section “NIST IR 7622”.

cards.question: Put the first five practices in the manual's order.
cards.answer:
1. Uniquely identify supply chain elements, processes, and actors
2. Limit access and exposure within the supply chain
3. Establish and maintain the provenance of elements, processes, tools, and data
4. Share information within strict limits
5. Perform supply chain risk management awareness and training
cards.explanation: Follow the thread: identify, limit access, track the origin, share little, train.

items: Uniquely identify supply chain elements, processes, and actors
Limit access and exposure within the supply chain
Establish and maintain the provenance of elements, processes, tools, and data
Perform supply chain risk management awareness and training

cards.question: Put the last five practices in the manual's order.
cards.answer:
6. Use defensive design for systems, elements, and processes
7. Perform continuous integrator review
8. Strengthen delivery mechanisms
9. Assure sustainment activities and processes
10. Manage disposal and final disposition activities throughout the system or element lifecycle
cards.explanation: Follow the thread: design to resist, review the integrator, deliver safely, keep up, and finish cleanly.

items: Use defensive design for systems, elements, and processes
Manage disposal and final disposition activities throughout the system or element lifecycle

cards.question: What does “provenance” mean in the practice “establish and maintain the provenance”?
cards.answer: Provenance is the origin and history of an item: where it comes from and who handled it along the way.
cards.explanation: Like the label on a product that says where it was made.
cards.explanation_more: This simple explanation is outside the manual: the book does not define the word.

cards.question: Which U.S. text is about national security systems?
options: CNSS Directive 505
CNCI initiative number 11
cards.answer: CNSS Directive 505
cards.explanation: Directive 505 sets requirements for national security systems. CNCI 11 gives tools to agencies.
cards.explanation_more: Source: official manual (ISC)2, Domain 1, section “NIST IR 7622”.

cards.question: What does “defensive design” mean in the list of practices?
cards.answer: Designing systems while expecting from the start that someone may attack them.
cards.explanation: Like a house designed from the plan with strong locks.
cards.explanation_more: This simple explanation is outside the manual: the book does not define the expression.

cards.question: Why are the actions not the same for every actor in the chain?
cards.answer: Because each actor has a different role. The manual says the actions, the level and the type of control change with that role.
cards.explanation: A small supplier and a big manufacturer do not have the same responsibilities.

cards.question: A small supplier and a big manufacturer apply NIST IR 7622 differently. Is that normal?
options: Yes: control depends on each one's role
No: everyone must apply the same controls
No: only the small supplier must adapt
options_why: The manual says the level and the type of control change with the role.
Both actors have a role, so both adapt their actions.
cards.answer: Yes: control depends on each one's role
cards.explanation: The text asks for actions that fit the role, not one single control for everyone.

cards.question: NIST IR 7622 identifies [[10|ten]] practices to consider when facing supply chain risk.
cards.answer: NIST IR 7622 identifies 10 practices to consider when facing supply chain risk.
cards.explanation: Ten, not twelve: twelve is the British NCSC.

cards.question: Which NIST IR 7622 practice is about the end of life of a piece of equipment or software?
cards.answer: Manage disposal and final disposition activities throughout the system or element lifecycle. In other words: manage disposal (getting rid of things safely) during the whole life cycle.
cards.explanation: It is the last practice on the list.

cards.question: What if your company throws away old hard drives without care?
cards.answer: Company data could leave with them. The last practice asks you to manage disposal during the whole life cycle.
cards.explanation: Security does not stop when you stop using a piece of equipment.

cards.question: Explain in your own words the practice “Share information within strict limits”.
cards.answer: Share information about the chain only with people who need it, and within strict limits.
cards.explanation: The fewer people who know, the less the information can leak.

cards.question: What does the CNCI initiative number 11 do?
cards.answer: It gives U.S. agencies tools to manage their cyber supply chain. The approach is based on risk (risk-driven).
cards.explanation: Practical tools, not only principles.
cards.explanation_more: Source: official manual (ISC)2, Domain 1, section “NIST IR 7622”. CNCI stands for Comprehensive National Cybersecurity Initiative.

concepts.name: ISO 28000: a framework for the supply chain

decouverte.titre: The coach who starts again every week
paragraphes: Your soccer team often loses. The coach prepares a plan, tests it in a match, looks at the result, then corrects it.
The coach starts again every week. The team slowly gets better, without changing everything at once.
Security standards use the same idea: the PDCA cycle (plan, do, check, act). An ISO standard is a text of good practices published by the international organization ISO.

decouverte.comme: Plan the training, do it, check the score, act to correct. Then start again.
decouverte.enVrai: PDCA stands for: Plan, make a plan. Do, carry it out. Check, verify the result. Act, correct what needs it. A company repeats this cycle to improve its security, round after round. The image stops here: a soccer season ends, but the PDCA cycle never stops.

decouverte.question: ISO 28000 is about the supply chain. Is it only for cybersecurity?
options: No: it is not specific to cybersecurity
Yes: it only talks about computer security
decouverte.answer: No: it is not specific to cybersecurity
decouverte.explanation: The manual says ISO 28000 is not specific to cybersecurity. It looks at the chain in general. Thinking it is only about computers is a natural reflex.

decouverte.titre: A standard that adds to the others
decouverte.texte: A company already follows ISO 9001 and ISO 27001, two other ISO standards. It adds ISO 28000 for its supply chain. Everything fits into its audits and its overall risk management.

cards.question: Official definition: “ISO 28000”
cards.answer: ISO 28000:2007, "Specification for security management systems for the supply chain," provides a broad framework for managing supply chain risk.
cards.explanation: ISO 28000: a broad framework for managing supply chain risk.
cards.explanation_more: Sentence from the official manual (ISC)2, Domain 1, section “ISO 28000”.

cards.question: ISO 28000:2007, "Specification for security management systems for the supply chain," provides a broad [[framework]] for [[managing]] supply chain risk.
cards.answer: ISO 28000:2007, "Specification for security management systems for the supply chain," provides a broad framework for managing supply chain risk.
cards.explanation: A framework for managing the risk.

cards.question: ISO 28000:2007, "[[Specification for security management systems]] for the supply chain," provides a [[broad framework]] for [[managing supply chain risk]].
cards.answer: ISO 28000:2007, "Specification for security management systems for the supply chain," provides a broad framework for managing supply chain risk.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: the title of the standard, the broad framework, managing the risk.

cards.question: Write the official definition of “ISO 28000” from memory.
cards.answer: ISO 28000:2007, "Specification for security management systems for the supply chain," provides a broad framework for managing supply chain risk.
cards.explanation: Start with the title of the standard, then “provides a broad framework”.

cards.question: Official definition: “PDCA” in ISO 28000
cards.answer: ISO 28000:2007 relies heavily on the continuous process improvement model of plan, do, check, act (PDCA) to improve the security management system and to assure organizational conformance to the security practice.
cards.explanation: PDCA: plan, do, check, act, then start again.
cards.explanation_more: Sentence from the official manual (ISC)2, Domain 1, section “ISO 28000”. Conformance means the organization really follows the security practice.

cards.question: ISO 28000:2007 relies heavily on the continuous process [[improvement]] model of plan, do, check, act (PDCA) to improve the security management system and to assure organizational [[conformance]] to the security practice.
cards.answer: ISO 28000:2007 relies heavily on the continuous process improvement model of plan, do, check, act (PDCA) to improve the security management system and to assure organizational conformance to the security practice.
cards.explanation: Two key words: improvement (you get better) and conformance (you follow the rules).

cards.question: ISO 28000:2007 relies heavily on the [[continuous process improvement]] model of [[plan, do, check, act]] (PDCA) to improve the [[security management system]] and to assure organizational conformance to the security practice.
cards.answer: ISO 28000:2007 relies heavily on the continuous process improvement model of plan, do, check, act (PDCA) to improve the security management system and to assure organizational conformance to the security practice.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: continuous improvement, the four steps, the management system.

cards.question: Write from memory the manual's sentence about “PDCA” in ISO 28000.
cards.answer: ISO 28000:2007 relies heavily on the continuous process improvement model of plan, do, check, act (PDCA) to improve the security management system and to assure organizational conformance to the security practice.
cards.explanation: Look for two goals: improve the system, and assure conformance.

cards.question: Official definition: who ISO 28000 is useful for
cards.answer: While not specific to cybersecurity, ISO 28000 is useful for organizations that leverage other ISO specifications (such as ISO 9001 and ISO 27001) to align supply chain risk with the organizations' audit processes or that seek to use a standardized, risk-based approach to evaluating supply chain risk.
cards.explanation: Two audiences: those who already follow other ISO standards, and those who want a standard method.
cards.explanation_more: Sentence from the official manual (ISC)2, Domain 1, section “ISO 28000”.

cards.question: While not [[specific to cybersecurity]], ISO 28000 is useful for organizations that [[leverage other ISO specifications]] (such as ISO 9001 and ISO 27001) to align supply chain risk with the organizations' audit processes or that seek to use a [[standardized, risk-based approach]] to evaluating supply chain risk.
cards.answer: While not specific to cybersecurity, ISO 28000 is useful for organizations that leverage other ISO specifications (such as ISO 9001 and ISO 27001) to align supply chain risk with the organizations' audit processes or that seek to use a standardized, risk-based approach to evaluating supply chain risk.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: not only for cyber, builds on other ISO standards, a standard approach.

cards.question: What do the letters PDCA stand for?
cards.answer: Plan, do, check, act: make a plan, do it, check the result, take action.
cards.explanation: Four verbs, always in this order.

cards.question: Put the four steps of the PDCA cycle in order.
cards.answer:
1. Plan (make a plan)
2. Do (carry it out)
3. Check (verify the result)
4. Act (correct)
cards.explanation: You prepare, you do, you look at the result, you correct. Then you start again.

cards.question: Is ISO 28000 a standard only for cybersecurity?
options: No, it is broader
Yes, only cybersecurity
cards.answer: No, it is broader
cards.explanation: The manual says it is not specific to cybersecurity. It deals with the security of the chain in general.

cards.question: Every three months, a company plans improvements, puts them in place, measures the results, then corrects. Which model does it follow?
options: Plan, do, check, act
Identify, protect, detect, respond
Avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept
Spoofing, tampering, repudiation
options_why: These are the first functions of a cybersecurity framework, not an improvement cycle.
These are the possible responses to a risk, not an improvement cycle.
These are types of threats, not an improvement cycle.
cards.answer: Plan, do, check, act
cards.explanation: Plan, do, check, act: this is the PDCA cycle, which ISO 28000 uses to keep improving.

cards.question: ISO 28000 relies on [[continuous]] improvement through the PDCA cycle.
cards.answer: ISO 28000 relies on continuous improvement through the PDCA cycle.
cards.explanation: A cycle you repeat, without ever stopping.

cards.question: Why does the PDCA cycle never stop?
cards.answer: Because risks and suppliers change. After acting, you check again and start over, to improve the system little by little.
cards.explanation: Security that stands still quickly gets out of date.

cards.question: According to the manual, what advantage does the PDCA cycle bring?
cards.answer: It makes it easier to join supply chain risk with the organization's wider risk management activities.
cards.explanation: The supply chain does not stay in a corner: it joins the overall management of risk.
cards.explanation_more: Source: official manual (ISC)2, Domain 1, section “ISO 28000”.

cards.question: What if a company follows no other ISO standard: can it use ISO 28000?
cards.answer: Yes. ISO 28000 is also useful for those who want a standard approach. This approach is based on risk.
cards.explanation: Other ISO standards are only one of the two uses named.

cards.question: Explain in your own words how a company would use PDCA to improve how it follows its suppliers.
cards.answer: It plans the checks, carries them out, verifies the results, then corrects what is not working. Then it starts again.
cards.explanation: Each turn of the cycle improves the follow-up a little.

concepts.name: The 12 principles of the U.K. NCSC (National Cyber Security Centre)

paragraphes: The school principal wants to choose suppliers well. The work is cut into four stages: know who delivers what, set rules, check, then improve.
A country did the same for companies: twelve principles, grouped into four stages.
These twelve principles come from the national cybersecurity center of the United Kingdom: the NCSC (National Cyber Security Centre).

decouverte.comme: To climb a staircase, you go from one step to the next. If you skip the first one, you may fall.
decouverte.enVrai: The four NCSC stages go in order: understand the risks, establish control, check your arrangements, keep improving. Each stage prepares the next one. The image stops here: after the last step, you keep on improving.

decouverte.question: You are in charge of your company's suppliers. Which stage do you start with?
options: I understand the risks: who are my suppliers?
I check my arrangements with them
I look for continuous improvement
decouverte.answer: I understand the risks: who are my suppliers?
decouverte.explanation: You cannot control or check what you do not know. First, you identify the suppliers and what needs protecting. The other stages come after.

decouverte.texte: Stage 1: the company lists its suppliers and what it must protect. Stage 2: it sets its minimum requirements and shares them. Stage 3: it plans audit rights and performance indicators (KPIs, numbers that show whether it works). Stage 4: it builds trust and encourages progress.

cards.question: Official definition: the “NCSC” and its principles
cards.answer: The U.K. National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) proposed guidance that attempts to provide organizations with improved awareness of supply chain risks, while also establishing 12 principles intended to help organizations establish and maintain effective control of their supply chain.
cards.explanation: Two goals: know the risks better, and keep control thanks to 12 principles.
cards.explanation_more: Sentence from the official manual (ISC)2, Domain 1, section “U.K. National Cyber Security Centre”.

cards.question: The U.K. National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) proposed guidance that attempts to provide organizations with [[improved awareness]] of supply chain risks, while also establishing [[12 principles]] intended to help organizations establish and [[maintain effective control]] of their supply chain.
cards.answer: The U.K. National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) proposed guidance that attempts to provide organizations with improved awareness of supply chain risks, while also establishing 12 principles intended to help organizations establish and maintain effective control of their supply chain.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: know the risks better, 12 principles, keep effective control.

cards.question: Official definition: NCSC stage 1, “Understand the risks”
cards.answer: Understand the risks: The principles in this stage involve identifying your vendors in your supply chain and establishing what needs to be protected in that supply chain (and why).
cards.explanation: Stage 1: who are my suppliers, and what must I protect?
cards.explanation_more: Sentence from the official manual (ISC)2, Domain 1, section “U.K. National Cyber Security Centre”.

cards.question: [[Understand the risks]]: The principles in this stage involve [[identifying your vendors]] in your supply chain and establishing what [[needs to be protected]] in that supply chain (and why).
cards.answer: Understand the risks: The principles in this stage involve identifying your vendors in your supply chain and establishing what needs to be protected in that supply chain (and why).
cards.explanation: Three blocks: the name of the stage, identify the suppliers, what must be protected.

cards.question: Official definition: NCSC stage 2, “Establish control”
cards.answer: Establish control: This stage involves establishing minimum security requirements (see the earlier section "Minimum Security Requirements") and communicating your security expectations to your suppliers.
cards.explanation: Stage 2: set the MSRs, then tell the suppliers clearly.
cards.explanation_more: Sentence from the official manual (ISC)2, Domain 1, section “U.K. National Cyber Security Centre”.

cards.question: [[Establish control]]: This stage involves [[establishing minimum security requirements]] (see the earlier section "Minimum Security Requirements") and [[communicating your security expectations]] to your suppliers.
cards.answer: Establish control: This stage involves establishing minimum security requirements (see the earlier section "Minimum Security Requirements") and communicating your security expectations to your suppliers.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: the name of the stage, the minimum requirements, the communication.

cards.question: Official definition: NCSC stage 3, “Check your arrangements”
cards.answer: Check your arrangements: This stage involves establishing assurance activities and building those into your supply chain processes.
cards.explanation: Stage 3: plan checks to be sure the rules are followed.
cards.explanation_more: Sentence from the official manual (ISC)2, Domain 1. The next sentence of the manual names audit rights, key performance indicators and other tests.

cards.question: [[Check your arrangements]]: This stage involves [[establishing assurance activities]] and [[building those into]] your supply chain processes.
cards.answer: Check your arrangements: This stage involves establishing assurance activities and building those into your supply chain processes.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: the name of the stage, the assurance activities, building them in.

cards.question: Official definition: NCSC stage 4, “Continuous improvement”
cards.answer: Continuous improvement: This stage involves continually building trust with your suppliers and constantly encouraging security improvements for your supply chain.
cards.explanation: Stage 4: trust and progress, every day.
cards.explanation_more: Sentence from the official manual (ISC)2, Domain 1, section “U.K. National Cyber Security Centre”.

cards.question: [[Continuous improvement]]: This stage involves [[continually building trust]] with your suppliers and [[constantly encouraging security improvements]] for your supply chain.
cards.answer: Continuous improvement: This stage involves continually building trust with your suppliers and constantly encouraging security improvements for your supply chain.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: the name of the stage, building trust, encouraging improvements.

cards.question: Put the four NCSC stages in order.
cards.answer:
1. Understand the risks
2. Establish control
3. Check your arrangements
4. Continuous improvement
cards.explanation: You understand, you set the rules, you check, then you keep improving.

cards.question: A company writes its minimum security requirements and sends them to its suppliers. Which NCSC stage is it in?
options: Establish control
Understand the risks
Check your arrangements
Continuous improvement
options_why: This stage is for identifying the suppliers and what to protect, before the rules.
This stage checks that the rules are followed, after they have been set.
This stage builds trust and encourages progress, after the other three.
cards.answer: Establish control
cards.explanation: Setting minimum requirements and sharing them means establishing control.

cards.question: In which stage does each action belong?
cards.answer: Understand the risks: list your suppliers, decide what must be protected. Check your arrangements: plan audit rights, set indicators. Continuous improvement: encourage progress, build trust.
cards.explanation: Understand = know. Check = control. Improve = make progress with the suppliers.

items.text: List your suppliers
Decide what must be protected in the chain
Plan audit rights
Set performance indicators (KPIs)
Constantly encourage security improvements
Slowly build trust with the suppliers

cards.question: How many principles does the NCSC propose, and in how many stages?
cards.answer: 12 principles, grouped into 4 stages.
cards.explanation: Twelve principles, four stages: do not mix them up with the ten NIST practices.
cards.explanation_more: Source: official manual (ISC)2, Domain 1, section “U.K. National Cyber Security Centre”.

cards.question: What does the “Check your arrangements” stage include, besides assurance activities?
cards.answer: Setting audit rights, key performance indicators (KPIs) and other testing and validation activities.
cards.explanation: Concrete ways to check that suppliers keep their word.
cards.explanation_more: Source: official manual (ISC)2, Domain 1, section “U.K. National Cyber Security Centre”.

cards.question: In the “Establish control” stage, you set the minimum requirements and you [[communicate]] your security expectations to the suppliers.
cards.answer: In the “Establish control” stage, you set the minimum requirements and you communicate your security expectations to the suppliers.
cards.explanation: A rule that the supplier does not know is useless.

cards.question: Why does the “Understand the risks” stage come first?
cards.answer: Because you cannot control or check suppliers you do not know. You must first identify them and know what you are protecting, and why.
cards.explanation: You cannot protect what you have not identified.

cards.question: What if a company skips the “Check your arrangements” stage?
cards.answer: It has rules and requirements, but it does not know whether the suppliers follow them. Audit rights and indicators are there exactly to check.
cards.explanation: A rule without checking stays a simple promise.

cards.question: Give a concrete example of an action for the “Continuous improvement” stage.
cards.answer: For example: talk every year with your suppliers about possible progress, and encourage them to improve their security.
cards.explanation: This stage builds trust and pushes suppliers to make progress.
